lead: Change one resistor in a solved circuit, or insert an ammeter, and every current shifts a little. The compensation theorem finds those shifts without solving the whole circuit again. It replaces the change by one small voltage source, the compensating source Vc = IΔZ, and the currents this source drives on its own are exactly the changes. Engineers use it to find the error an ammeter causes, the effect of a resistor's tolerance or ageing, and the effect of a fault or a change of load. Only a few syllabi list it, and where it is listed it is examined with the other network theorems, for DC and AC circuits.

blocks.text: In a linear network, let a branch of impedance Z carry a current I. If that impedance changes to Z + ΔZ, the change in the current of every branch equals the current that a voltage source Vc = IΔZ would produce in that branch, when

items: V<sub>c</sub> is placed in series with the changed branch (which now has Z + ΔZ), with its polarity opposing I: + where I enters the branch, like the extra drop IΔZ;
every independent source is switched off (voltage sources shorted, current sources opened, internal impedances kept);
dependent sources are left in place.

blocks.text: Then each new current is the old current plus the change. For DC circuits Z is a resistance R and ΔZ a resistance change ΔR. A current-source form exists too (a current source V ΔY across a branch whose admittance changes), but the voltage form above is the one examined. The theorem is built on the substitution theorem: any branch whose voltage and current are known can be replaced by a source of that voltage (or current) without changing anything else in the network.

items: Look into the network from the two ends of the branch. The rest of the network is V<sub>th</sub> behind Z<sub>th</sub>, so the original current is I = V<sub>th</sub>/(Z<sub>th</sub> + Z).
After the change the current is I′ = V<sub>th</sub>/(Z<sub>th</sub> + Z + ΔZ).
The change is ΔI = I′ − I = V<sub>th</sub>[(Z<sub>th</sub> + Z) − (Z<sub>th</sub> + Z + ΔZ)]/[(Z<sub>th</sub> + Z)(Z<sub>th</sub> + Z + ΔZ)].
Simplify, using V<sub>th</sub>/(Z<sub>th</sub> + Z) = I: ΔI = −IΔZ/(Z<sub>th</sub> + Z + ΔZ).
That is exactly the current a source IΔZ, opposing I, drives round a loop of impedance Z<sub>th</sub> + Z + ΔZ, which is the compensation network with the independent sources off.
Every other branch current is a linear response to the same change, so by superposition its change is the current the same source drives in that branch.

blocks.text: The minus sign says an increase in impedance (ΔZ positive) reduces the branch current, as expected. The result also explains when the change is small: if ΔZ is much less than Z<sub>th</sub> + Z, the relative change ΔI/I is about −ΔZ/(Z<sub>th</sub> + Z).

items: Solve the original circuit for the current I in the branch that will change (often it is already known).
Draw the compensation network: switch off the independent sources, put Z + ΔZ in the branch, and put V<sub>c</sub> = IΔZ in series with it, + where I enters.
Solve this one-source circuit for the changes ΔI in the branches you need.
Add each change to the old current, and check one current by solving the changed circuit directly.

blocks.text: Ammeter error. An ammeter of resistance RA inserted in a branch is a change ΔR = RA. The meter therefore reads I + ΔI instead of I, and the compensation theorem gives the error at once (worked example 2). AC circuits. The theorem holds for phasors with complex Z and ΔZ (see applying network theorems to AC circuits); then Vc = IΔZ is a phasor too.

examples.question: A 30 V source in series with 2 Ω feeds a 6 Ω resistor in parallel with a 3 Ω branch (Figure 2.7.1). The 3 Ω resistor is replaced by 4 Ω. Use the compensation theorem to find the change in the current of each branch, and check by solving the changed circuit.
steps: Original circuit: 6 ∥ 3 = 2 Ω, so the source sees 2 + 2 = 4 Ω and supplies 30/4 = 7.5 A. The 3 Ω branch carries I = 7.5 × 6/9 = 5 A and the 6 Ω carries 2.5 A.
Change: ΔR = 4 − 3 = 1 Ω, so V<sub>c</sub> = IΔR = 5 × 1 = 5 V, opposing the 5 A.
Compensation network: short the 30 V source. V<sub>c</sub> sees the 4 Ω in series with 2 ∥ 6 = 1.5 Ω, a total of 5.5 Ω.
Change in the changed branch: ΔI = 5/5.5 = 0.909 A against the original current. New current: 5 − 0.909 = 4.091 A.

This 0.909 A splits between the 2 Ω and the 6 Ω: 0.909 × 2/8 = 0.227 A through the 6 Ω, in the same direction as its original 2.5 A, and 0.909 × 6/8 = 0.682 A through the 2 Ω, against the source current.
Direct check: 6 ∥ 4 = 2.4 Ω, the source sees 4.4 Ω and supplies 30/4.4 = 6.818 A; the 4 Ω takes 6.818 × 6/10 = 4.091 A and the 6 Ω takes 2.727 A. All three agree.
examples.answer: The changed branch falls from 5 A to 4.091 A, the 6 Ω rises from 2.5 A to 2.727 A, and the source current falls from 7.5 A to 6.818 A.

examples.question: In the original circuit of worked example 1 (30 V, 2 Ω, 6 Ω in parallel with 3 Ω), an ammeter of resistance 0.5 Ω is inserted in the 3 Ω branch to measure its 5 A. What does it read, and what is the error?
steps: The ammeter adds ΔR = 0.5 Ω to a branch carrying I = 5 A, so V<sub>c</sub> = 5 × 0.5 = 2.5 V.
Compensation network: 30 V source shorted; V<sub>c</sub> drives the 3.5 Ω branch in series with 2 ∥ 6 = 1.5 Ω, total 5 Ω.
ΔI = 2.5/5 = 0.5 A against the original current, so the ammeter reads 5 − 0.5 = 4.5 A.
Error: 0.5/5 = 10 % low. In general the reading is I(R<sub>th</sub> + R)/(R<sub>th</sub> + R + R<sub>A</sub>), here 5 × 4.5/5 = 4.5 A with R<sub>th</sub> = 1.5 Ω and R = 3 Ω.
Direct check: 6 ∥ 3.5 = 2.211 Ω; the source supplies 30/4.211 = 7.125 A; the meter branch takes 7.125 × 6/9.5 = 4.5 A.
examples.answer: The ammeter reads 4.5 A instead of 5 A, an error of 10 % caused by its own 0.5 Ω.

traps: Using the new current I′ in V<sub>c</sub> = IΔZ together with the changed impedance Z + ΔZ. With Z + ΔZ in the compensation network, V<sub>c</sub> uses the original current I.
Leaving the original sources on in the compensation network. Only V<sub>c</sub> acts; every independent source is switched off.
Giving V<sub>c</sub> the wrong polarity. It opposes the original current (+ where I enters), so a larger resistance always reduces that branch current.
Forgetting that the changes spread to other branches. In worked example 1 the 6 Ω current rises by 0.227 A even though that resistor did not change.
Switching off a dependent source in the compensation network. It stays, as in every theorem of this unit.

quiz.a: In a linear network, if a branch impedance Z carrying current I changes to Z + ΔZ, the changes in all currents are the currents produced, with all independent sources off, by a voltage source IΔZ in series with the changed branch, opposing I.

quiz.q: Why must the compensating source oppose the original current?
quiz.a: It stands for the extra voltage drop IΔZ that the added impedance causes in the direction of I. An added drop pushes against I, so the source is + where I enters the branch.

quiz.q: In worked example 1 the 3 Ω branch is changed to 2 Ω instead. Find its new current by compensation.
quiz.a: ΔR = −1 Ω, so V<sub>c</sub> = 5 × (−1) = −5 V: it now aids the current. ΔI = 5/(2 + 1.5) = 1.429 A in the direction of I, so the new current is 6.429 A. Check: 30/(2 + 6 ∥ 2) = 8.571 A, and 8.571 × 6/8 = 6.429 A.

quiz.q: A branch carries 2 A; the rest of the network seen from it plus the branch itself total 10 Ω. A 2.5 Ω resistor is added in series. Find the change in the branch current.
quiz.a: ΔI = −IΔR/(R<sub>total</sub> + ΔR) = −2 × 2.5/12.5 = −0.4 A. New current 1.6 A.

quiz.q: A branch Z = 4 + j3 Ω carries I = 2∠0° A, and the rest of the network seen from the branch is Z<sub>th</sub> = 2 − j3 Ω. A reactance ΔZ = j2 Ω is added. Find the new current.
Show that an ammeter's percentage error depends on the ratio of its resistance to the resistance round the measured loop.
quiz.a: Reading = I(R<sub>th</sub> + R)/(R<sub>th</sub> + R + R<sub>A</sub>), so the error is R<sub>A</sub>/(R<sub>th</sub> + R + R<sub>A</sub>) of the true value. In worked example 2: 0.5/5 = 10 %. A 0.05 Ω meter in the same place: 0.05/4.55 = 1.1 %.

beyond: The compensation idea grows into sensitivity analysis: circuit simulators report how much each output changes per ohm of each resistor, and tolerance or Monte Carlo analysis uses those numbers to predict the spread of a production batch. Power-system engineers use the same idea, under the name compensation method, to update a solved network quickly when a line is switched out. Search for 'sensitivity analysis SPICE', 'tolerance analysis' and 'compensation method contingency analysis'.
